analysis.one_liner: Requires independent third-party testing and certification that toys for young children meet federal safety standards.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Consumer Product Safety Act to require every manufacturer of a product for a child under age five to have it tested and certified by an independent lab, separate from the maker, confirming it meets federal safety standards or is not a banned hazard [S2]. Toys without that certificate could not be imported into the United States [S2]. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and caregivers of children under five, who would gain an independent check that toys meet federal safety rules before they reach store shelves, and independent testing laboratories, which would gain the testing business the bill mandates.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers of products for children under 60 months would have to certify, based on testing by a nongovernmental independent third party, that each product conforms to federal safety standards or is not a banned hazardous product [S2].
The independent tester must be physically separate from, and not owned or controlled by, the manufacturer whose product it tests, so companies could no longer certify their own toys [S3].
Children's products lacking the required third-party certification could not be legally imported, keeping uncertified toys out of the U.S. market at the border [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Toy manufacturers, importers, and private labelers, who would bear the cost of third-party testing and certification for every covered product; some of that cost would likely reach consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The testing requirement would fall on manufacturers and importers of every covered product, a cost that falls hardest on smaller firms and would likely be passed partly to consumers through higher prices [S3].
The bill's coverage is limited to products intended for children under 60 months of age, leaving toys and articles aimed at older children outside the mandatory third-party testing requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: independent testing adds cost to a low-margin, import-heavy industry, but it directly addresses a product category where a safety failure can poison or injure a small child. The bill was narrow and focused, though its under-five age cutoff left a gap for older children's products.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Ferguson introduced the Safe Toys for Kids Act on September 5, 2007, joined as an original cosponsor by Rep. Edolphus Towns [S1].
Four representatives cosponsored the bill, split between one Democrat and three Republicans [S4].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction and then to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection; the record shows no further action, hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy manufacturers and importers avoided the third-party testing costs this bill would have imposed. Families gained nothing from this bill, though Congress enacted comparable third-party testing requirements for children's products in the broader consumer product safety law passed the following summer (widely reported; not in the provided sources).

for.name: Rep. Mike Ferguson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring third-party testing and certification of young children's toys.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor joined by one Democrat and three Republicans — and no vote was ever taken on it, so there was never a partisan roll to divide [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required independent third-party testing and certification for every product aimed at children under five, and barred imports without it. The industry's cost savings from the bill dying came at the price of families not getting an independent safety check on toys — a category hit by major lead-paint recalls that year.
The bill created a mandated customer base: every covered children's product would need testing by an independent lab physically separate from the maker. Its death also meant no new business.
Retailers and brands that sell toys under their own labels would share the certification obligation with manufacturers, adding compliance costs. The bill's defeat spared them that expense.
